result: Cataract-treated participants showed impaired sensorimotor recalibration immediately after surgery compared to age-matched sighted controls, but their recalibration performance was significantly greater than zero.
evaluation: Claims C5, C28, C38, and C39 provide converging evidence from statistical analyses showing that cataract-treated participants recalibrated significantly less than both control groups (p≤0.006) but still showed significant recalibration above zero (p=0.0012). The experimental design with appropriate controls and statistical tests supports this finding.

result: The impaired recalibration in cataract-treated participants cannot be explained solely by reduced visual acuity, as sighted controls with experimentally matched visual blur still recalibrated faster.
evaluation: Claims C6 and C86 are supported by the experimental design (C141-C143) that included a CSF-matched control group with artificially blurred vision. The finding that blur-matched controls still outperformed cataract-treated participants demonstrates that visual acuity alone does not account for the deficit.

result: Recalibration ability in cataract-treated participants gradually improved over time after surgery, following an exponential time course with a time constant of ~1.5 years, reaching the level of blur-matched controls at approximately 2 years post-surgery.
evaluation: Claims C7, C47, C48, C49, C88, C117, and C123 collectively demonstrate longitudinal improvement with statistical support (p=0.04) and exponential modeling (b=1.5, CI=[0.51, 2.49]). The finding is robust to exclusion of long-term participants (C50), though the authors acknowledge substantial uncertainty due to inter-subject variability.

result: Baseline pointing precision (variance) negatively correlated with recalibration performance in cataract-treated participants, but this sensorimotor noise cannot fully explain the improvement over time since noise levels remained constant while recalibration improved.
evaluation: Claims C40, C41, and C72 show significant negative correlations between baseline variance and recalibration (r=-0.53, p=0.019 for irecal; r=-0.47, p=0.035 for Adaptation). Claims C97 and C98 demonstrate that while cataract-treated participants had higher baseline noise, this noise did not change over time despite improved recalibration, ruling out noise reduction as the sole mechanism.

result: Visual acuity (CSF cutoff frequency) positively correlated with recalibration performance in cataract-treated participants.
evaluation: Claims C42, C73, and C87 report significant positive correlations between visual acuity and recalibration measures (r=0.5, p=0.025 for irecal; r=0.54, p=0.014 for Adaptation). However, claim C44 notes that visual acuity did not correlate with time since surgery, and C88 shows recalibration improved without corresponding visual acuity improvements, indicating visual acuity is not the sole factor.

result: Time since surgery positively correlated with recalibration performance in cataract-treated participants.
evaluation: Claims C43 and C74 demonstrate that participants tested longer after surgery showed better recalibration (r=0.55, p=0.02 for Adaptation; r=0.60, p=0.013 for Aftereffect). This is consistent with the longitudinal improvement findings and supports the role of post-surgical experience.

result: Recalibration performance correlated with multisensory integration ability in cataract-treated participants tested in both tasks, suggesting both abilities may depend on establishing correspondence between sensory and sensorimotor maps.
evaluation: Claims C52 and C115 report a significant correlation (r=0.58, p=0.03) between recalibration and multisensory integration in 14 participants. However, claims C116 and C125 acknowledge this is correlational evidence and the mechanistic interpretation remains speculative. The correlation is intriguing but does not establish causality or shared mechanisms definitively.

result: Cataract-treated participants did not show the typical trial-by-trial decay of the aftereffect in the post-prism phase that was observed in sighted controls, suggesting impaired use of proprioceptive feedback for recalibration.
evaluation: Claims C60-C62 demonstrate that sighted controls showed significant aftereffect decay (b=-0.11 and b=-0.04) while cataract-treated participants did not (CI included 0). Claims C65, C89, and C90 confirm this difference. The interpretation regarding proprioception (C91-C95) is supported by the task design (no visual feedback in post-prism phase) and prior literature (C63, C67).

result: Cataract-treated participants could accurately point to targets at baseline (pre-prism phase) with accuracy comparable to controls, but showed significantly reduced precision (higher variance) compared to both control groups.
evaluation: Claims C53-C58 provide comprehensive statistical evidence that cataract-treated participants had comparable accuracy (p=0.61) but significantly higher variance than both control groups (p<0.0001). The regression analysis (C58) confirms they could correctly perform the task across different target positions (slope=1), establishing that basic visuomotor mapping was present.

result: The development of recalibration ability requires visual and sensorimotor experience rather than age or visual acuity alone, as demonstrated by comparing cataract-treated participants with age-matched and younger sighted controls.
evaluation: Claims C83-C85 demonstrate that age is not the sole factor by showing 13-year-old cataract-treated participants performed worse than 6-7 year-old sighted controls. Claims C118, C122, and C124 draw the conclusion that early visual experience is necessary but the ability can develop with post-surgical experience. This is supported by the longitudinal improvement data and control comparisons.

result: In a subset of 4 participants tested before and shortly after surgery, visual acuity improved immediately post-surgery but recalibration performance did not, with significant improvement only occurring 4-16 months later.
evaluation: Claims C46 and C47 describe longitudinal data from 4 participants showing dissociation between immediate visual acuity improvement and delayed recalibration improvement (p=0.04 for improvement at 4-16 months). This provides direct within-subject evidence that visual acuity improvement alone is insufficient for recalibration development.

result: In sighted controls, age positively correlated with recalibration performance, with older participants showing more efficient recalibration.
evaluation: Claim C75 reports a significant positive correlation (r=0.30, p=0.0007) in 124 sighted participants aged 6-35 years. This establishes the normal developmental trajectory against which the cataract-treated participants' performance can be compared.

result: The youngest sighted controls (6-7 years old) already showed aftereffect decay during the post-prism phase, unlike cataract-treated participants, indicating the cataract-treated group's behavior is less mature than age-matched sighted peers.
evaluation: Claims C68 and C69 provide specific evidence that even the youngest sighted controls (n=11, 6-7 years) showed significant aftereffect decay (b=-0.1, CI=[-0.17,-0.03]), which cataract-treated participants (mean age 13 years) did not show. This supports the interpretation of developmental delay rather than simple age effects.

result: The experimental paradigm consisted of three phases: pre-prism baseline (neutral goggles, no visual feedback), prism adaptation (20 prism diopters rightward shift, terminal visual feedback), and post-prism aftereffect (neutral goggles, no visual feedback).
evaluation: Claims C29-C36 comprehensively describe the experimental procedure with appropriate methodological details. The paradigm is well-established (C29 cites similar methods) and the terminal feedback approach is validated by prior work (C34). The design appropriately tests both adaptation and aftereffect components of recalibration.

result: Twenty Ethiopian children and adolescents with dense congenital bilateral cataracts were surgically treated on average 11.5 years after birth, with post-surgical vision remaining poorer than normal despite treatment.
evaluation: Claims C128-C139 provide comprehensive participant characterization including demographics, clinical diagnosis criteria (optical nystagmus, family history, strabismus), surgical treatment details, and visual outcomes. The diagnosis of congenital cataracts is well-supported by multiple clinical indicators and the poor post-surgical outcomes are consistent with cited literature on late treatment.

result: Two control groups were tested: 20 age-matched sighted participants with normal vision, and 20 age- and visual-acuity-matched sighted participants tested with experimentally induced blur.
evaluation: Claims C140-C142 describe the control group design. The inclusion of both normal-vision and blur-matched controls is methodologically sound for isolating the effects of visual acuity from other factors. The matching procedure is described in detail and validated by CSF measurements.

result: All three groups (cataract-treated, sighted controls, sighted with blur) differed significantly from each other in recalibration index.
evaluation: Claim C37 reports significant omnibus test (χ²(2)=27, p<0.0001, η²=0.38) followed by pairwise comparisons (all p≤0.006). The statistical approach is appropriate with Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons, and the effect size is substantial.

result: Adaptation and Aftereffect are correlated but potentially separate phenomena relying on different neural networks.
evaluation: Claim C70 reports significant correlation (r=0.47, p=0.037) between the two measures, while C71 cites literature suggesting they may involve different neural mechanisms. This justifies analyzing them separately while acknowledging their relationship.

result: The lack of early pattern vision affects visuomotor recalibration, but the ability is not permanently lost and can develop with sufficient post-surgical experience even after many years of visual impairment.
evaluation: Claims C8, C9, and C127 represent the main conclusions of the study, supported by the collective evidence of initial impairment (C5, C38), improvement over time (C7, C47, C48), and the role of experience rather than age alone (C83, C84). The conclusion is well-supported by the experimental data and control comparisons.

result: The main deficit in cataract-treated participants appears to be in recalibrating sensorimotor mappings when perturbed, potentially due to difficulty establishing correspondence between visual, proprioceptive, and motor spaces.
evaluation: Claims C100, C104, and C108 propose mechanistic explanations for the observed deficits. While C104 is supported by the data showing intact baseline pointing but impaired adaptation, C100 and C108 are explicitly speculative (evidence_type includes SPECULATION). The proposed mechanism is plausible but not directly tested.

result: Cataract-treated participants could accurately localize and reach for targets shortly after surgery, and some could even perform the task before surgery, indicating they had developed or could quickly develop basic sensorimotor mappings.
evaluation: Claims C101 and C102 are supported by the baseline performance data (C53, C57, C58) showing accurate pointing despite higher variance. The observation that 4 participants could perform the task pre-surgically (C45) provides additional evidence that some visuomotor mapping can develop even with limited vision.

result: The exponential fit of recalibration improvement over time is not driven by the two participants tested more than 10 years after surgery.
evaluation: Claim C50 reports a control analysis showing that excluding the two long-term participants yields a comparable time constant (b=1.5, CI=[0.39, 2.67]) to the full sample. This demonstrates the robustness of the exponential improvement finding.
